scope: Independent targeted source review of scripts, translations, selected material and everyday-life claims, and endings. This is not a full audit of all 39 sources.
result: No blocking factual error found in checked passages. One wording precision recommendation; one manuscript locator remains partially verified because the publisher PDF repeatedly returned 502.

findings.issue: The translated epitaph says that Shahidullah respected scholars, widows and orphans. The current 'praises support for' can suggest documented financial or practical assistance beyond that wording.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace 'Its translated epitaph praises support for scholars, widows and orphans.' with 'Its translated epitaph praises his regard for scholars, widows and orphans.'
findings.locator: Object description, translated epitaph in section 4

sourcesChecked.details: Hebrew excerpt and English meaning match recto left line 7. Catalog calls the manuscript a copy attributed to a Khazar Jew. Serah appears in recto left lines 13 to 16; Joseph's marriage to an Alan ruler's daughter appears in verso left lines 12 to 14. The card appropriately attributes these narratives to the letter.

Article 1(1) exactly matches the Bulgarian sample. The translation is accurate. Direct HTML opening returned no extracted text, but the official indexed page and Parliament's scanned 1991 publication corroborate the sentence.

Catalog explicitly transcribes the Arabic words, identifies a probable Volga-Bulgar imitation naming Nasr II, gives ruler dates 914 to 943, and says the uniface coin lacks mint and date. Card preserves the uncertain attribution and distinguishes Arabic from spoken Bulgar. The script is supported by the catalog transcription, not an independently deciphered image.

Publisher abstract supports ninth-century nonliterary Greek in Bulgar inscriptions. Indexed PDF text confirms the exact title/name sequence and the Turdatzis funerary passage. Repeated full-PDF openings returned 502, preventing independent confirmation of inscription 66, printed page 353, limestone material, and the particular line break. No contradictory evidence found; retain the drafting agent's page-level check if it has the PDF.

Museum supports eighth-century dating, five engraved imitation stamps, uncertain Avar or Byzantine manufacture, possibly copied Greek inscription, competing explanations for the Vrap group, and defeat in Charlemagne's campaigns around 800.

Abstract and introduction support 424 sampled people, four cemeteries, about 300 linked individuals, nine generations, patrilocality and female exogamy, ancestry memory inference, and arrival in 567 to 568. The card's limited geographical generalization and distinction between biological and social kinship are appropriate.
Supports 1317, limestone, goldsmith Shahidullah, Arabic script and museum identification of language as Tatar. Original script was not independently transcribed from the image.

Supports second half of thirteenth century, copper alloy/red copper/silver, Arabic wish for success and wellbeing, and expensive accessory under Golden Horde rule. Original Arabic is not provided in readable transcription, so the new coin sample is the better supported script example.

Russian text explicitly identifies five fourteenth-century public baths, social function, Red Chamber changing-room stone seats, washing rooms, boilers/furnace, underfloor heating and ceramic water/drainage pipes. Card correctly distinguishes this from the independent pre-conquest state.

Abstract supports named cemetery sites, metal/glass/wood form parallels, early to mid-eighth-century emphasis, and four Topola pottery kilns. The card avoids turning stylistic resemblance into proof of imported objects.
Museum supports tenth-century St Theodore icon, Patleina excavations in 1909, 12 by 12 centimetre tiles, local monastic workshops, dark outline, red slip and colored glaze.

Discussion distinguishes chronicle date 965 from Ibn Hawqal's 968 to 969 destruction, returning refugees, and brief political remnants. Card appropriately avoids claiming one precise disappearance date for all Khazars.

Supports Bulgarian authorities' deportation of more than 11000 Jews from occupied Macedonia, Thrace and Pirot, almost all murdered at Treblinka, alongside persecution, forced labor, confiscation and Sofia expulsions in the core territory. USHMM's companion Axis Powers article also explicitly supports protests and widespread opposition to the plan.

otherLimits: Did not independently recheck every chronology claim, every source budget, or map identity and geometry.
No additional Volga gravestone or inkwell original-script excerpt supplied: readable scholarly transcription was unavailable, and guessing from an image would be inappropriate.
The Avar undeciphered-language limitation is appropriate and should remain.
